chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated to me from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab from Safwan ibn Yahya from Kulayb al-Saydawi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

It is written in the Torah that My houses on earth are the mosques. So, good news to a servant who purified himself in his house, then visited Me in My house. Indeed, upon the visited one is the honor of the visitor. And in another hadith: Good news to those who walk in the darkness to the mosques with bright light on the Day of Judgment.

key_terms.التَّوْرَاهِ: The Torah, referring to the scripture of Prophet Moses (AS)
key_terms.الزَّائِرِ: The visitor, referring to the worshipper visiting the mosque/God
key_terms.النُّورِ السَّاطِعِ: The bright light, a metaphor for guidance and reward on the Day of Judgment
key_terms.الْمَزُورِ: The visited one (God), referring to the one being visited by the worshipper
key_terms.الْمَشَّاءِینَ: Those who walk, referring to those traveling to the mosque
key_terms.بُیُوتِی: My houses, referring to God's houses (mosques)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for walking to the mosque in darkness according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this hadith to link the physical act of mosque visitation with the spiritual concept of 'Ziyarat' (visitation) of the Imam, framing the mosque as the earthly house of the Divine. It specifically highlights the virtue of traveling to mosques in darkness, promising radiant light on the Day of Judgment, a theme deeply rooted in Shia eschatology regarding the guidance of the faithful. The narration also draws upon the Torah to establish the universality of mosques as God's houses, reinforcing their sanctity across Abrahamic traditions.
